entry.title: Tiny Galaxy in the Milky Way's Halo
entry.summary: Using data from the future Vera Rubin Observatory, astronomers have found Aquarius IV — a very small and faint stellar system. It lies far away, in the galactic halo, and consists of ancient stars. Its properties resemble those of a dwarf galaxy, but it could also turn out to be a globular cluster. Deeper observations are needed to tell for sure.

entry.title: Catching the Moment a Protein Breaks
entry.summary: Proteins constantly fold and unfold, and this determines how they work. To understand this process, you need a special coordinate that shows how close a protein is to the transition. Previously, it was very difficult to compute. Now, a method has been devised that finds this coordinate from one-dimensional profiles using already available data. This speeds up calculations and helps better understand how proteins work.

entry.title: How Strain Alters the Run of Dark Particles in a Crystal
entry.summary: In two-dimensional semiconductors such as WSe₂, the lowest-energy states are dark excitons. They don't emit light directly, but they govern the thermal motion of particles and the faint glow at low temperatures. Scientists have for the first time traced how mechanical stretching or compressing the material changes the speed and character of hot exciton motion in the first moments after excitation. It turns out that stretching sharply accelerates the particles' run, while compressing makes it oscillate rhythmically. These microscopic details open the way to controlling the properties of future chips with simple deformation.

entry.title: A Quantum Lego Set for Superconductivity
entry.summary: Scientists tested a theory that predicted superconductivity in artificial layered materials. They built a superconducting 'sandwich' from alternating layers of copper oxide and a metal. By varying the layer thicknesses, they could smoothly transition from weak to strong superconductivity and back. The behavior traces a dome, with the peak marking the best conditions for superconductivity. This control paves the way for new superconducting devices and possibly materials that work at higher temperatures.

entry.title: A Cosmic Accelerator with No Brakes
entry.summary: In the early universe, a special field—the axion—could act like a pump, driving electromagnetic waves to enormous strengths. The back-reaction of these waves on the field itself was thought to be too violent for precise description. The authors discovered that for large coupling strengths, there is a wide range where everything remains tractable. This finding simplifies testing the theory against the cosmic microwave background and lifts some constraints on inflationary models.

entry.title: The Heart of a Black Hole: Why a Smooth Center Isn't Everything
entry.summary: Physicists often draw black holes without a singularity—with a smooth, finite center. But the authors of this work showed that one picture isn't enough. You need to check whether the theory behind such a hole can pass any infalling matter through the center without breaking. They derived a simple rule—a kind of stress test. It turns out that the popular Bardeen model fails this test, while the Hayward hole passes.

entry.title: A Pendulum That Feels Gravity Quantumly
entry.summary: Physicists suspended a tiny pendulum weighing 7 mg from a stepped fiber of fused silica. Gravitational dilution reduced mechanical losses, and structural damping with its 1/f noise was bypassed using a trap that shifts the resonance upward. This achieved a record suspension gain of Gq ≈ 2.5, exceeding the threshold needed for quantum entanglement of pendulums. The work paves the way for macroscopic quantum experiments with objects visible to the naked eye.

entry.title: Quantum Waves in the Macroworld: A Hair-Thin Wire
entry.summary: Quantum phenomena are usually confined to tiny particles. Here, scientists created a nearly perfect one-dimensional conductor where electrons behave like waves and maintain quantum order over a distance comparable to the thickness of a human hair. A special low-temperature setup revealed discrete energy levels, strict spin ordering, and a complex interference pattern. This is a step toward understanding where the microcosm ends and the familiar macrocosm begins.

entry.title: Plasma on a Leash: How to Design a Particle Trap
entry.summary: Stellarator fusion reactors lose hot particles due to their complex three-dimensional shape. Previously, the shape was optimized based on indirect indicators rather than actual particle motion. The authors created a computational method that directly calculates how particles fly in the magnetic trap. The result is compact reactor designs with excellent fast-ion confinement and plasma stability. The method for the first time unifies orbit physics and engineering constraints in a single workflow.

entry.title: A Quiet Diamond Film
entry.summary: Scientists have grown ultra-pure diamond layers with special defects—nitrogen-vacancy centers. These centers act as tiny magnetometers. Previously, adding nitrogen caused disorder that interfered with measurements. The authors found a way to deliver nitrogen smoothly, without jumps, and obtained a film with record-low noise. Such material paves the way for highly sensitive sensors in chemistry and biology.

entry.title: Hidden Accelerator in the SS 433 Jet
entry.summary: Astrophysicists studied the magnetic field in the jet of the microquasar SS 433 near the black hole. They found that the field decays more slowly than expected, meaning the magnetic rigidity increases with distance. This allows protons to be accelerated to 2.6 PeV—just enough to explain the gamma-ray emission from this system. The discovery points to a previously unknown natural accelerator inside the SS 433 outflows.

entry.title: X-ray Beacons Spawn Ghost Particles
entry.summary: Astrophysicists examined the coronae of ultraluminous X-ray sources—systems where a black hole devours matter at an enormous rate. Calculations show that under certain conditions, protons in the corona are accelerated to high energies and produce neutrinos. These particles barely interact with matter and can travel to Earth, carrying information about distant objects. The source M82 X-1 in a neighboring galaxy looks particularly promising. Future neutrino telescopes may be able to catch its signal.

entry.title: The Black Hole and Its Secret Twin
entry.summary: Mathematicians have found a hidden symmetry in the equation describing the vibrations of space around a rotating black hole. This symmetry links the original black hole to another, 'dual' black hole. It turns out that the twin is also a black hole, but with different properties. The discovery offers a fresh perspective on the stability of black holes and the geometry of spacetime itself.

entry.title: A Full-Body Scan Told Us About Future Diseases
entry.summary: Researchers built a model called LeDXA that finds hidden signs of whole-body health in DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) scans. The model was trained on 11,000 unlabeled scans, learning patterns on its own. It turned out that such scans predict disease risk better than standard measurements of density and body composition. LeDXA also estimated biological age and showed that hormone therapy may slow it down.

entry.title: How Dust Disks Dance Around Newborn Stars
entry.summary: Scientists simulated how disks of gas and dust grow around young stars. It turns out that matter often falls not gently but in dense 'streams'—streamers. These streamers can deliver as much mass in 10,000 years as the usual inflow over the entire period, and temporarily compress the disk by half. In early epochs, such turbulence prevents particles from sticking together into planets. Later, when the flow calms down, the disk is fed through its midplane and outer layers, and the magnetic field organizes into a ring with reversals.

entry.title: Comet Dust: A View from Orbit and the Lab
entry.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope studied comet 81P/Wild 2—the same comet whose dust was brought back by the Stardust probe in 2006. The NIRSpec and MIRI spectrometers detected water vapor, carbon dioxide, and organic molecules. The comet's composition matched previous flyby data, while dust analysis revealed a mix of amorphous carbon and olivine crystals. Comparison with Stardust samples confirmed that the two methods see different populations of dust grains, complementing each other.

entry.title: Crackling in quantum processor silenced for seconds
entry.summary: Superconducting quantum processors harbor parasitic defects—two-level systems. They cause energy loss and instability. Scientists have developed an ultrafast spectroscopy method showing these defects switch and drift within seconds. Previously, such processes were thought to be slow, taking hours. This finding forces a rethink of how quantum computers are calibrated.

entry.title: Dark Matter Around a Black Hole: A Torus-Shaped Cloud
entry.summary: Scientists have studied how ultralight dark matter particles gather around a rotating black hole. They accounted for both the black hole's spin and the interactions between particles. It turns out the cloud takes the shape of a torus, not a sphere, and its properties depend on a single simple number. This helps us understand how dark matter behaves near black holes.

entry.title: Superconductivity Withstood Pressure of 210 Gigapascals
entry.summary: Physicists studied superconductivity in a free-standing membrane of strontium-doped lanthanum nickelate under ultrahigh pressure. The material withstood compression up to 210 gigapascals (about 2 million atmospheres) without losing its superconducting state. The transition temperature first rose, peaking at 74.5 kelvin at 146 gigapascals, then gradually declined. Such resilience to ultrahigh pressure has never been seen before in oxide superconductors.

entry.title: Division That Doesn't Fragment Memory
entry.summary: Standard neural networks struggle to hold smooth, continuous values in memory—they tend to discretize them into steps. The authors built a network that uses divisive (rather than subtractive) signal normalization, mimicking real neurons. This allows the network to smoothly update its stored signal without losing precision. They found that division naturally constrains learning into a narrow channel, avoiding chaos. This approach explains why the brain might rely on this specific biological mechanism.

entry.title: The Nitrogen Trail of a Shredded Star
entry.summary: Astronomers caught rare repeating X-ray flares from AT2019wzc. Its spectrum shows a nitrogen absorption line, while lines of other elements are nearly absent. This suggests the black hole tore apart a nitrogen-rich star, like an aged Sun. The discovery links two puzzling phenomena: tidal disruption events and quasi-periodic eruptions.

entry.title: The Dim Glow of Black Holes Won't Save the Universe
entry.summary: Astronomers tried to reconcile the two main ways of measuring the cosmos—by ancient light and by galaxy distribution. There's a slight mismatch: the galaxy map shows a bit less matter than the ancient light map predicts. The idea was to add a scattering fog of evaporating primordial black holes. It would slightly blur the ancient light map and bring the numbers closer. But calculations showed the effect is too weak to fix anything.

entry.title: Ultra-precise clocks compared over distance
entry.summary: Physicists compared the ticking of two atomic clocks: one based on an ytterbium ion, the other on strontium atoms. The measurements lasted nearly two years, and the clocks matched to within just 4.3 × 10⁻¹⁸. That's three times more precise than previous experiments. Such precision is needed to redefine the second and to measure altitude by the passage of time.

entry.title: Smartwatches vs. Sugar: Why the Accuracy Was a Mirage
entry.summary: Scientists have created the first reproducible method for testing algorithms that predict blood sugar levels from pulse signals (photoplethysmography). They evaluated five popular methods on shared data using three types of data splitting: random, subject-wise, and subject-exclusive. With random splitting, models seemed accurate, but under more honest tests, their predictions were no better than simply predicting the mean. Moreover, nearly all predictions fell into clinically acceptable zones on the standard error grid, even for a deliberately useless model. This shows that common medical metrics can hide algorithm failure, creating a false sense of reliability.

entry.title: Quantum Mpemba effect: how hot cools faster than cold
entry.summary: On two independent neutral-atom quantum processors, the quantum Mpemba effect was observed for the first time in an open system. Engineered initial states set either a fast or a slow relaxation path. The fast path opened access to previously unreachable physics of mixed states, while the slow path revealed hidden defects in state preparation and control. Measurements in the computational basis directly assessed the processor's reliability, turning the dynamics itself into a calibration tool.

entry.title: How to Catch the Gravitational Tremor of a Dying Star
entry.summary: Astrophysicists applied deep learning to extract the signal of a rapidly spinning core-collapse supernova from detector noise. It turns out that combining several detectors into a network not only helps pinpoint the explosion's parameters but also widens the zone from which we can hear it. For current facilities, the core's 'ring' frequency is discernible up to 30,000 light-years, while the spin rate and strength can be picked out from a hundred thousand. Next-generation detectors will push this horizon ten times farther.

entry.title: A Leaky Bucket Doesn't Quench a Cosmic Maser
entry.summary: Astronomers have figured out why molecular clouds sometimes flare up like giant radio beacons. In such systems, the upper energy level can discharge through two paths: a slow working one and a very fast parasitic one. A model showed that a fast leak doesn't suppress amplification if there's an excess of excited molecules in the working transition. This explains the nature of mysterious methanol maser flares.

entry.title: The Universe Isn't Chasing Entropy Records
entry.summary: This article examines whether the Universe truly takes the fastest path to chaos via black holes. It turns out it doesn't. Although black holes contribute nearly all entropy, their actual growth rate is thousands of times slower than theoretically possible. This means galaxy and star formation doesn't obey a principle of maximum disorder speed.

entry.title: Two Signals in the Universe's Noise
entry.summary: Gravitational waves from merging black holes and neutron stars create a collective hum—the gravitational wave background. Scientists applied deep learning to extract this background from the noise of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detectors. The new method not only finds the signal but also splits it into a part from astrophysical sources and a part from processes in the early universe. This paves the way for detecting gravitational waves born right after the Big Bang.

entry.title: Dark Vortices Dampen Drag
entry.summary: Astrophysicists have found that ultralight dark matter, when spun into a vortex, exerts much weaker drag on passing star clusters. The key is a match in velocities: if the cluster and the vortex move in the same direction, the braking force drops dramatically. This explains the mystery of the dwarf galaxy Fornax, where clusters haven't fallen to the center as fast as old models predicted. The discovery changes our view of how invisible matter governs the motion of stars.

entry.title: A Cosmic Collider in an Inflating Universe
entry.summary: During cosmic inflation, the expansion of space itself acts as a particle accelerator. The scalar field (inflaton) generates an electric field in an extra dimension. This field produces charged particles via an analog of the Schwinger effect, and neutral particles through special interactions. Even particles heavier than the Hubble scale appear without the usual suppression. This opens a path to testing grand unified theories through relic signals.

entry.title: Neural Network Teaches Gravity Not to Hide
entry.summary: The authors built a neural network emulator that predicts in fractions of a second how dark matter inhomogeneities change under modified gravity. Previously, such calculations took hours; now they take moments. The emulator was tested on synthetic data and recovered cosmological parameters with high accuracy. This is an important step in preparing for new large-scale sky surveys that will look for deviations from Einstein's theory.

entry.title: Dark Photons from a Wobbling Field
entry.summary: Physicists have revisited the birth of dark photons—candidates for dark matter. In this model, the dark Higgs field randomly deviates from its equilibrium during inflation, and as it decays, it produces a stream of fast dark photons. Calculations show that this scenario is possible for particles with masses from 100 eV to 1 GeV and very weak interaction strength. Future observations of the cosmic microwave background or distant hydrogen clouds could test this idea.

entry.title: The Universe Heats Up on Vortices
entry.summary: In theories of gravity with spacetime torsion, inflation (the ultra-fast expansion of the early Universe) may be driven not by a special field but by the dynamic torsion itself. It naturally couples to Standard Model particles, so the reheating process after inflation proceeds differently. The authors calculated how the inflaton (the particle responsible for inflation) decays and found that particle production via quantum anomalies gives a significant contribution. This sets a lower bound on the reheating temperature and changes our understanding of how the Universe became hot.

entry.title: Camera Jitter Blurs Our View of Alien Worlds
entry.summary: Astronomers are trying to directly photograph planets outside our solar system, but the bright glare of the star and optical disturbances spoil the images. In a new study, researchers propose using data from adaptive optics sensors to better remove these disturbances. A slight mismatch in jitter between the camera and the sensors currently hampers the effort, but the scientists already know how to measure and correct it.

entry.title: Dark Matter from Magnetic Droplets
entry.summary: The authors built a model where dark matter consists of magnetic monopoles that formed as the hot universe cooled. Normally, too few such particles are produced, but adding a light dark fermion suppresses its abundance, making monopoles the dominant component. Their mass is about one hundred million gigaelectronvolts, beyond the reach of current detectors. However, the model predicts a distinctive dark radiation and gravitational waves that future observatories might detect.

entry.title: Magnetic Hearing at Kilohertz Frequencies
entry.summary: Scientists have proposed improving a gravitational wave detector based on a magnetic bar. Instead of a uniform field, they used a special magnet arrangement (Halbach array) that creates strong field gradients with less overall strength. This allows detecting very short and weak signals at frequencies from 10 kilohertz to a megahertz—where conventional detectors are blind. Sensitivity could reach 10⁻²¹ 1/√Hz, and with upgrades, even 10⁻²³ 1/√Hz.

entry.title: How Orbits Reveal the Universe's Curvature
entry.summary: Scientists compared how almost circular orbits change in classical physics and in general relativity. They derived exact formulas for the perihelion shift—the point of closest approach—and found conditions under which the orbit remains closed. It turns out that even a tiny cosmological constant can affect this shift. The authors also discovered a rare case where the shift disappears entirely.

entry.title: Black Hole Echo: What the Horizon Sounds Like
entry.summary: Physicists are studying the echoes of gravitational waves from exotic compact objects—ghostly stand-ins for black holes. It turns out that the frequency of these reflections isn't constant; instead, they cluster according to a hyperbolic law. This clustering depends only on the external curvature of space, not on the object's internal structure. The discovery offers a new way to peer beyond the event horizon.

entry.title: Birth of Dark Matter in the Inflationary Furnace
entry.summary: Physicists have studied how light dark photons—a special type of dark matter particle—could have arisen from quantum fluctuations during cosmic inflation. They showed that the changing properties of space during that period strongly influence the final abundance of such particles. Using the Starobinsky model of inflation as an example, they calculated that to explain the observed dark matter, the dark photon mass must lie between 5.6 and 7.4 microelectronvolts. This narrow mass window provides a clear target for future experiments.

entry.title: A Black Hole's Shadow with a Secret from Other Dimensions
entry.summary: Astrophysicists have studied what a black hole looks like in a universe model with extra dimensions. They accounted for the hole's rotation, the observer's tilt, and the 'tidal charge'—a property absent in ordinary black holes. It turns out the image becomes strongly asymmetric: the inner shadow deforms, and the brightness of the rings depends on the observation frequency. The results will help future telescopes search for traces of hidden dimensions in real images.

entry.title: Ripples in the Fabric of the Early Universe
entry.summary: Physicists investigated how stable bubbles of energy, called oscillons, form during the rapid expansion of the universe (inflation). They found that under certain conditions, these clumps generate gravitational waves with a frequency of about 25 billion hertz. Such a signal is too weak to violate known cosmological constraints, but it could be detected by future experiments using resonant cavities. This opens a new way to peer into an era from which no other traces remain.

entry.title: How Black Holes Spit Out Energy
entry.summary: Scientists simulated how stellar-mass black holes devour matter at extreme rates. It turns out that up to 90% of the material is blasted back out as winds and jets, and the strength of these outflows depends on the black hole's spin and the rate of fuel supply. The black hole's mass has no effect. Rapid spin dramatically boosts the efficiency of energy extraction, and the radiation is beamed into a narrow cone, making such systems appear ultra-bright to distant observers.

entry.title: Three Faces of the Cosmos: Geometry, Growth, and the Beginning
entry.summary: The standard cosmological model ΛCDM (cold dark matter and dark energy) does an excellent job describing most observations, but a few discrepancies have emerged. To stress-test the model, researchers split the influence of three different epochs: the geometry of space, the growth of large-scale structure, and the physics of the early Universe. They found that geometry and the early Universe give different values for the density of matter—a difference of about two standard deviations. Meanwhile, structure growth agrees with both. This could hint at hidden tensions in our understanding of the cosmos.

entry.title: Where Did Matter Come From? A Fresh Look at the Boltzmann Equation
entry.summary: In the first moments after the Big Bang, nearly equal amounts of matter and antimatter should have completely annihilated each other. But a tiny imbalance in favor of matter persisted — otherwise galaxies and stars would never have formed. A new study offers a more rigorous derivation of the Boltzmann equation for this process. The authors included corrections from particle interactions, making the calculation systematic. This brings us closer to understanding how a tiny bit of matter survived and became the visible universe.

entry.title: How Chaos Gives Birth to Life: The Secret Switch
entry.summary: In a computer model of the primordial 'soup', scientists observed how random collisions of molecules give rise to ordered chains. They measured a special property of the mixture—'causal influence', i.e., its ability to influence its own future. When this influence crosses a critical threshold, self-copying molecules spontaneously appear in the soup. By controlling this influence, one can extend or shorten the lifespan of such copiers. The discovery hints at how life might have arisen from chaos—and how it might be controlled.

entry.title: Mosaic on the Surface of a Black Hole
entry.summary: Physicists have proposed a general method for calculating the hidden information in black holes by dividing their surface into tiny identical cells. It turns out this information consists of two parts: the main one, proportional to the area, and a fixed constant correction. This approach relies on minimal assumptions and explains why black holes 'remember' information precisely on the surface. It's a step toward understanding the quantum nature of spacetime.

entry.title: Light Fringes Betray a Photon’s Spin
entry.summary: Two centuries ago, Arago and Fresnel noticed that light waves produce fringes only when they oscillate in the same plane. Now physicists have repeated the experiment with quantum states. They mixed an ordinary laser beam with a single photon, twisted either to the left or to the right. By measuring brightness and polarization, they saw that the fringe pattern depends on the photon’s spin direction. So a way to determine its internal rotation purely optically — just by looking at the picture — was born. The discovery will be useful in quantum networks and cryptography.

entry.title: Gravitational Waves in a Noisy Room
entry.summary: A precise correspondence has been established between the description of weak gravitational waves in an expanding universe and the well-known Caldeira–Leggett model of open systems. This reduces complex equations to one: a generalized Langevin equation for the gravitational wave. The influence of matter is captured by a single function—the spectral density. This approach opens the door to quantizing gravitational perturbations and the stochastic dynamics of spacetime.

entry.title: The Invisible Pattern of Dark Energy Across the Sky
entry.summary: In the 'kinetic gravity braiding' (KGB) model, dark energy and gravity are far more tightly linked than usually assumed. For the first time, the researchers used computer simulations to create full-sky maps for this case. They found that the bending of light and shifts in its frequency can deviate from standard predictions by tens of percent. This means next-generation telescopes will be able to pick up fine details on the sky map that betray dark energy's true nature.
